t: Resource Allocation and Political Campaigns: Notes towards a Methodology
abs: The research, the initial stages of which are presented here, is based on three observations concerning the nature of ‘advanced’ capitalist societies. In the first place, where one lives can have an important influence on one’s level of living (quality of life, life chances, real income). The growing volume of studies organized around territorial social indicators has shown the existence of wide disparities within small areas, leading to the development of concepts of territorial justice and injustice and to attempts at modelling the causes of such variation. Secondly, the state is becoming increasingly involved in the production and maintenance of real incomes; its function as a productive institution, generating employment and providing a wide range of public goods, far outweighs its original protective function. Finally, there is competition between groups of actors whose aim is to capture the power involved in operating the productive state. According to Miliband’s thesis, whichever of these groups of actors (political parties) is in power in a ‘western’ democracy, the institutions of capitalism will maintain control of the economy.

t: Contingency Theory and Public Bureaucracies
abs: The study of organizational bureaucracies has in recent years taken the form of ‘contingency theory’ a theory which rests upon the assumption that organizational characteristics have to be shaped to meet situational circumstances. The theory implies that the extent to which an organization secures a ‘goodness of fit’ between situational circumstances and structural characteristics will determine the level of organizational performance. Child summarizes it as follows: contingency theory ‘regards the design of an effective organization as necessarily having to be adapted to cope with the “contingencies” which derive from the circumstances of environment, technology, scale, resources and other factors in the situation in which an organization is operating’. It is interesting that not one of the major contributions to contingency theory has considered the existence of elected representatives, to whom an organization is subordinated, and who are themselves accountable to a wider electorate, as being a significant contingency operating upon government bureaucracies. Blau has studied several government agencies in the United States, covering personnel agencies finance departments and employment security agencies; Meyer examined finance authorities; Hage and Aiken studied sixteen social welfare agencies; Hall and Pugh et al. covered both public and private bureaucracies.

t: The Dynamics of Education Finance in Federal Systems: Cross-time Analyses
abs: This article is concerned with the cross-time patterns of relationships between education funding, social change, and intergovernmental relations in four federal systems. The basic hypothesis of the research reported here is that the policy processes of the four federations – Canada, the Federal Republic of Germany, Switzerland, and the United States – are essentially similar. That is, the determinants of certain fiscal outputs of the policy processes are the same across the set of four nations. Not only do we hypothesize that the determinants of levels of education expenditures will be the same across the systems, we also predict that expenditure changes over time will be produced by similar forces across the subnational jurisdictions of all four countries. The comparability hypothesis will be examined and tested in several ways. We are first interested in expenditure differentials across the subnational units (provinces, Länder, cantons, and states) and how these differentials have changed in recent years. Second, we shall examine the policy impact of socioeconomic differences and change in these differences across subnational units. Finally, we will explore the patterns of change in fiscal responsibility among subnational and local governments, along with the determinants and some of the effects of that change.

t: Twenty-six Outputs in Search of a Taxonomy
abs: Most recent public policy research has taken the public policy as the pivotal point rather than the end point of analysis. The research has attempted to ‘explain’ a particular policy output by specifying the process from which it emerged or by identifying the antecedent factors which seem to have caused the policy output. Other research has attempted to characterize the impacts of a public policy upon its environment. But the enthusiasm to move to the interesting questions of causes or effects seems to have left a theoretical and empirical vacuum around the concept of public policy itself. An indicator of this vacuum is the absence of an empirically tested taxonomy of public policies. References to policy taxonomies in the existing literature assume, at least implicitly, that there are different types of public policy allocations. Discussions often contain an homage to Lowi‘s classification of policies by their impact: distributive, redistributive, or regulatory. Occasionally there is a citation of Froman’s adaptation of the economists’ notion of divisibility of goods as either ‘areal’ or ‘segmental’ policy or Williams and Adrian’s categorization of local services as ‘amenity’, ‘caretaker’, or ‘promotional’.

t: In This Issue
Policy and Dramaturgy: A Critique of Current Conceptions of Policy Making
abs: Rationalism has ceased to be merely one style in politics and has become the stylistic criterion of all respectable politics (Oakeshott, Rationalism in Politics) Oakeshott’s observation applies a fortiori to the prevailing mode in the preoccupation of policy analysts, in the rhetoric of policy-making and in the administrative changes typical of more than a decade of governmental reform in the United Kingdom. The terms ‘rationality’ and ‘efficiency’, for example, figured prominently in the associated policy debates of those years and they are particularly characteristic, and perhaps even peculiarly reminiscent now of that period. However, the legacy of that mode in terms of the prevailing conceptualization of policy-making remains with us. It is the principal purpose of this paper to explore the ‘characteristic features of that conceptualization and examine the scope and function of the dramatic effect and symbolism which it has employed. No sustained attempt will be made here to detail a comprehensive alternative to this conceptualization. Before this can be done a preliminary attempt has to be made to specify the distinctive attributes of the approach – its particular traditions, peculiar preoccupations and specific outlook – so that its general appeal can be undermined.

t: The Expenditure-Financing Decision in British Local Government
abs: Using British data from the past two decades, this essay deals with two inadequacies in much of the analysis of local government spending. The first is that spending alone does not represent the full complexity of any official decision for it fails to relate spending decision to revenues. The second is that political influence is brought to bear on both these dimensions of the expenditure finance decision. Economic decline in many of the industrial democracies has made this choice much clearer. Major cities are threatened with bankruptcy as their debt becomes unmanageable and their resources are depleted. As these choice have become increasingly difficult, the partisan political differences that relate to both spending and finance have come to the surface. Recent studies have attempted to deal with each decision separately. Few have analysed economic and political determinants within a framework which recognizes the simultaneous nature of expenditure and finance decisions. (For a notable exception see Jackson’s paper.) Our analysis attempts to integrate these efforts using a simultaneous equation model. Like all local representatives, the Labour and Conservative councillors have different attitudes toward the extraction of private wealth in order to provide public services and benefits.

t: Planners, Policies and Organizational Boundaries: Some Recent Developments in Britain
abs: Strategic planners everywhere must seek to acquire two very different, but essentially complementary, types of skill. Not only must they be able to penetrate and to analyse complex issues of urban and regional development and change; at the same time, they must be able to understand, and work within, an intricate decision-making context of interacting agencies, professions and political forces. Whatever skills planners may develop in this direction are rarely recognized so explicitly as their technical skills of strategic analysis: but planners in many countries are becoming increasingly concerned to accord them fuller recognition in the professional and theoretical foundations of their work. In Britain, this question has recently been thrown into sharper relief by two important changes in the planners’ working environment, which have separate origins but have been unfolding in parallel, with important interactions between them. The first of these changes was in the statutory procedures of development planning, where the traditional Development Plans – the main statutory instrument both for detailed land zoning and for expression of broader policy positions – were replaced in 1968 by new statutory procedures, which sought to distinguish more clearly between the broader and the more local levels.

t: Uncertainty, Prices and the Supply of Housing
abs: The dramatic rise in house prices which occurred during the period 1971-73 focussed the attention of economists, politicians and the press on the operation of the private housing market, previously a rather neglected area of economics. The fundamental reason for the rise in prices was that, during the period, the effective demand for dwellings for owner-occupation far exceeded the supply coming onto the market. Whilst the nature of such a disequilibrium position is of little interest in itself, it is necessary to identify and understand the circumstances which gave rise to its existence if it is to be avoided in the future. The link between the lending behaviour of building societies and the rise in house prices has been the focus of attention of commentators and analysts. The period 1969-70 was one in which building societies were relatively short of funds and they were obliged, therefore, to restrict the number of mortgages advanced, with a consequent reduction in the level of effective demand. When funds began to flow once more into the societies they were able to expand their mortgage lending, increasing both the number and the value of these advances, and pent-up demand pressures were released.

t: InThis Issue
Citizen Surveys for Local Governments: A Copout, Manipulative Tool, or a Policy Guidance and Analysis Aid?
abs: More and more local governments in the United States appear to be sponsoring surveys of randomly selected samples of the community population. For the most part the surveys have been on a one-time basis for some special purpose (such as for transportation studies or for housing condition inventorying). Only rarely have such surveys been undertaken at periodic intervals with similar questions so that the effects of changes in policies and programs can be assessed and that time trends be identified. The research community, the federal government, national polling firms and some universities have ongoing, periodically repeated surveys such as the current population survey and health interview survey, which do obtain time series information on a variety of topics. Properly administered surveys conducted annually are a potentially very useful management tool for local governments. Why should a city or county government undertake surveys, particularly on a regular basis? The citizen survey has a very appealing characteristic. It is a means for obtaining citizen inputs into government programs and policies that is probably considerably more representative of the whole population than inputs from other sources (except, perhaps, elections) and without the volatility of information sometimes present in other approachcs.

t: Using Budget Pies to Reveal Preferences: Validation of a Survey Instrument
abs: Why use a budget pie? A classic problem faccs everyone who is curious about the perferences of at least one other individual: How can some simple questions lead us to accurately know about another’s preferences? Husbands and wives sometimes face this problem when they are trying to find out where the other would like to vacation, what type of Christmas present the other would like, and so on. Some spouses try to hide their own prefercnces, deferring instead to the preferences of the other. Some married couples end up doing something neither partner prefers, both of them believing they are doing the thing the other most wants. In the market-place, the entrepreneur faces the problem of ascertaining what his customers prefer. A misjudgement on his part will result in a loss of sales and profit. Continued difficulty in determining others’ prefcrences will result in business failure. But a private entrepreneur does have some information to go on. As private consumers purchase goods, they reveal their preferences for certain goods at one price over other goods at other prices. In the short run, quid pro quo relationships reveal much about the preferences of buyers for the goods and services they are currently offered.

t: The Democratic Response of Urban Governments: An Empirical Test with Simple Spatial Models
abs: Among the normative concerns of social scientists, one of the greatest lacunae is evaluation of government performance in light of populist democratic criteria. While formal theorists have continued elaborating models of a competitive political process, and while the search for an appropriate and serviceable welfare criterion goes on, the empirical application of our existing descriptive and prescriptive insights mostly waits in abeyance. This paper offers one attempt to apply formal criteria to the evaluation task. We first briefly develop several low-level, admittedly non-complex, statements about the expected outcome of public sector activity according to the median preference model. The model’s descriptive statements then serve as evaluative and comparative criteria as we test its adequacy under several assumptions concerning democratic responsivencss. Finally we attempt to explain variations in the degree of responsiveness exhibited by ten American urban governments by reference to three aspects of political structures. The value of our approach emanates, we believe, not from any new insight into the formal interpretations and predictions provided by positive political theorists. Rather, we consider the approach a nascent attempt to match formally derived expectations to non-experimental data from both public opinion surveys and aggregate characteristics of large American cities.

t: Measures of Citizen Evaluation of Local Government Services
abs: In recent research on local government efforts have been made to suggest and/or construct policy output or decision-making models that bring together several types of data. This paper seeks to specify such models by broadening the data base so that resource allocation is not simply predicated on previous expenditure patterns or simple relationships based on the cost of a unit of service. According to James Coleman, the need for multiple sources of data is among the principles that should govern policy research. For policy research, the criteria of parsimony and elegance that apply in discipline research are not important; the correctness of the predictions or results is important, and redundancy is valuable. The methodological factors supporting that propostion dictate the use of multiple sources of data and multiple methods of data analysis. The object of this paper will be to address Coleman’s policy principle from an intermediate and necessarily narrower perspective: we review thc utility of incorporating survey data into models studying the outputs of local government, stressing questions related to measurement. Researchers at the Urban Institute have been developing municipal service models conceptualizing productivity measurement in terms of several types of input measurements.

t: The Capabilites of Voting Rules in the Absence of Coalitions
abs: This paper discusses the features of a variety of rules that might be used to make group choices. The rules are evaluated under an assumption that coalitions have no impact, as might be true when the number of voters is large and secret ballots are used. The contributions of a number of writers are discussed in a framework that exposes new relationships among a variety of ideas. Some conditions that bear on the merit of a voting rule are as follows: Are all choices to be made between pairs of alternatives, or will some choices have to be made over three or more options? If there are multiple options, are they easily located in a Euclidean space? Is it essential that the voting rule involve relatively little calculation, or can it require extensive use of a computer? Is it necessary to treat all voters equally, or can the votes of some be weighted more heavily than those of others? Is there any readily identifiable basis for determining such weights? Could the voters be trusted to reveal intensities of preferences, to be used as weights, or would they behave erratically or strategically if asked to do so?

t: Modes of Collective Decision-Making: Eight Criteria for Evaluation of Representatives, Referenda, Participation and Surveys
abs: This short paper seeks more to raise questions than provide answers. It differs from most recent work on measuring citizen preferences in the range of questions posed. Indeed, most such work, we argue, represents what economists term suboptimizing. The major studies on social welfare functions deserve our respect for their mathematical elegance. But how is this tradition to be linked to more general concerns, such as assessing legislative decision-making versus citizen participation versus surveys? This paper outlines a framework that might be applied in a general benefit-cost approach. If its answers, in the form of entries in Table 1, are only most tentative, it still points to a distinctive set of questions for future work, In the meantime, policy makers and their consultants must reach decisions regarding the relative merits of such things as citizen surveys. This framework may serve minimally as a structure for assessment of alternatives. Table 1 lists four decision-making modes and eight criteria for their evaluation. The remainder of the paper comments briefly on the various cells of Table 1. The four modes in Table 1 are singled out because of their empirical frequency.

t: Utility and Collectivity: Some Suggestions on the Anatomy of Citizen Preferences
abs: This paper is an attempt to link certain public choice theories with empirical analysis of citizen preferences. We begin with a reasonably clear, or at least strong, relation: cities with more Irish, Catholic, and foreign-born residents spend more through their municipal budgets. The relation holds across three data sets for American cities: for 51 cities from 1880 to 1968, for 154 cities in 1903, and for 661 citics in 1960. Why? Clark tested and rejected a Downsean interpretation of this relation using data for ten cities and for Boston. His test was based on analysis of questionnaire items concerning preferred spending levels. This paper presents an alternative conceptualization for some of the same findings, by extending the basic Downsean framework to encompass distinct sectors within a political system. The basic elements of the public choice tradition are well known. We mention only one or two highlights to show how the present paper extends this framework. Economists concerned with public choice, from Buchanan, Tullock, Downs, and Olsen have largely operated with an assumption of methodological individualism.

t: Comments on Preference Revelation for Public Policy Decisions
abs: 1. These are good papers. I found them rewarding. I shall have some remarks for all three, but most of this discussion refers to the Tideman and Clark papers (not, however, for reasons of quality). This Tideman paper is an exceptionally full survey, and very well done. There is solid analysis and reasonable judgement. It is quite a useful work. The Clark paper is most helpful to the reader in providing a great deal of background very clearly, The situational distinctions among the dimensions of public policy and citizen attitudes are especially illuminating. Both papers explicitly specify criteria for evaluating different public decision rules. In view of the fact that these are often only implicit in public policy analysis, a potentially highly misleading procedure when there is such a variety of rules to examine, this overtness is an important strength. Besides these rather similar general attractions, the Clark paper emphasizes that ‘measuring instruments … (should be) … only as precise and complex as necessary for the decision at hand’. Since precision and complexity entail sometimes considerable cost to investigators or policy officials, this inherently economic principle is hard to resist.

t: Introduction
Editors’ Note
Municipal Expenditures in Norway: Autonomy and Constraints in Local Government Activity
abs: The purpose of this article is to test some propositions about the effect of local ‘needs’, resources and political variables on municipal expenditures in 460 Norwegian communes. We have made use of a ‘means-end’-model of local autonomy to differentiate between municipal policies. We assume that the range of local discretion will vary along at least two dimensions: (1) the degree of local independence in framing the goals of the municipal activities, and (2) the latitude left to the municipal authorities concerning the means for fulfilling the defined goals. Four policy areas are chosen, each illustrating different categories of the model. The results of regression analyses between per capita expenditures in the four policy areas and the independent variables indicate that while resources account for a substantial part of the variation in expenditures in all policy areas, ‘needs’ seem to be important determinants in those areas where goals are prescribed by central government. Political variables exert an independent impact on the level of expenditures in those areas of policy where the municipalities enjoy some degree of autonomy on one of the two dimensions in the model. In the most autonomous area, however, only resources seem to be of importance in determining the expenditure levels.

t: The Politics of Community Planning for The Elderly
abs: The research focused on: (1) characteristics of organizations and individuals involved in planning and their perspectives of the problems of aging; (2) the activities of the planning organizations, and (3) the contribution to planning activities and outcomes made by economic, status, or power interests of planning members. Study conclusions are that planning activities are dominated by ‘agingspecific’ organizations and their members. Planning activities are characterized by organizational and interorganizational conflicts in which the organizations and professionals involvcd attempt to legitimate and ‘professionalize’ their work in aging, partially as a means of dealing with their lack of rcsourccs and threatened organizational survival. The data indicate that both the nature and task of planning (conceptualized in broad and ambiguous terms) and the structure of the planning organizations (essentially federative) combined to prevent: (1) the objective identification of gaps and needs in the field of aging as a basis for ‘planning’; (2) the inclusion of members representing multiple professions, community organizations or institutions, or the elderly themselves, or (3) social action. Thus, in the politics of planning the planning organizations become a vehicle for relatively weak organizations to deal with their basic survival needs. Major implications of study findings in the light of present national legislation and policy in aging are discussed.

t: Floaters, Loyalists and the Independence of Swing and Partisanship
abs: A model of movers and stayers (‘floaters’ and ‘loyalists’) is outlined (Section 1) in which the transitions and the floaters between one period and another are independent of the position (party or abstention) supported at the earlier time period. This model has some empirical support as a good first approximation to recent British voting behaviour. The conditions under which a national process of this kind can be seen as the aggregation of such processes operating at the constituency (or subgroup) level are established (Section 2). The extension of this model over a succession of time periods is seen to create no problems (Section 3). In Section 4, using a slight extension of the assumptions of Section 2, the (approximate) independence of swing and partisanship is seen as a natural consequence of the model and it is argued that the assumptions used are reasonable in the post-war British context.

t: Councillors’ Attitudes Towards New Town Development Corporations
abs: This article outlines the results of a survey of councillor’s attitudes towards new town development corporations. The historical background of the origin and development of new town corporations shows how the present policy conflicts have arisen. The survey of councillors gives for the first time the local representatives’ opinions and attitudes about the development corporations. The main finding is that although the development corporation is thought to be a good generator of growth, substantial changes in policy are desired. The councillors feel that when the new towns are completed they should be handed over to the local authorities. There is greater feeling against the ‘undemocratic’ structure of the development corporation in the more prosperous south of the country. In the north the attitude tends to be that the development corporations are acceptable so long as they tangibly benefit the area. Conservatives tend to be in favour of the development corporations because they act as a check on local Labour councils. Labour councillors tend to be in favour of the idea of a development corporation where the need is clear, but oppose what is seen as their development into undemocratic outposts of the bureaucracy. Finally, what most councillors want is a greater degree of participation in the decisions made by the development corporations.

t: Diversity Within the Total Institution: Some Evidence from Boys’ Perceptions of Community Homes
abs: Some residential institutions allow staff considerable autonomy in the day-to-day running of the organization, while others curtail this freedom by imposing strong central control. One of the important differences between these two types of organization is the degree of diversity experienced by the residents. Taking a sample of community homes for delinquent boys, this study examines diversity within their welfare and work subsystems and also within houses and working groups. Two conclusions are reached: first, the more diverse the welfare and work subsystems, the less conflict is there between instrumental and expressive goals: secondly, the greater the diversity between house units within a community home, the more supportive the staff are seen to be.
